nameStory: The eastern lampmussel gets its name from its shell's distinctive rays that radiate outward from the hinge like beams of light from an old oil lamp. The word 'lampmussel' comes from this lamp-like appearance, while 'eastern' distinguishes it from similar species found in other parts of North America.
description: The eastern lampmussel is a freshwater clam that lives buried in sandy or muddy river and stream bottoms throughout New England. Its oval shell typically measures 2-4 inches long and displays beautiful radiating green or yellowish rays against a brown or olive background. Like all freshwater mussels, it's a filter feeder that helps clean the water by straining out tiny particles and algae. You'll usually only see the edge of its shell peeking above the sediment, or find empty shells washed up on shore.

idTips.label: Radiating rays
idTips.description: Look for distinct green or yellow rays that spread outward from the hinge area like spokes on a wheel - these feel smooth to the touch and are the mussel's signature feature

idTips.label: Oval shell shape
idTips.description: Shell is elongated and egg-shaped, feeling solid and heavy in your hand with a slightly curved profile when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Shell color
idTips.description: Background color ranges from olive-brown to yellowish-brown with a slightly glossy surface that may feel gritty from algae growth

idTips.label: Interior nacre
idTips.description: Inside surface is smooth, pearly white with a rainbow sheen that feels slippery when wet - this mother-of-pearl lining is iridescent

idTips.label: Growth rings
idTips.description: Concentric rings visible on the shell surface feel like gentle ridges under your fingertip, similar to tree rings showing years of growth

habitat: Eastern lampmussels live in clean, flowing rivers and streams with sandy or gravelly bottoms throughout New England's watersheds. They prefer areas with moderate current where they can burrow partway into the sediment while still accessing flowing water for feeding. You'll find them in the Connecticut River system, Merrimack River, and other major waterways where water quality remains good.

seasonality.spring: Mussels become more active as water warms, extending their feeding tubes (siphons) more frequently. This is peak reproduction season when they release larvae.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for feeding and growth. Look for siphon holes in sandy shallows or find shells along shorelines after summer storms.
seasonality.fall: Activity slows as temperatures drop. Empty shells from natural mortality become more visible as water levels often recede during dry autumn weather.
seasonality.winter: Mussels remain buried and largely inactive under ice. Shell collecting is easiest now when many streams have low, clear water.

funFact: Eastern lampmussels are master manipulators that trick fish into raising their babies - they disguise their larvae-filled egg sacs to look like tasty worms or small fish, and when a bass or other fish tries to eat the fake bait, thousands of tiny mussel larvae clamp onto the fish's gills for a free ride to new territory!
confusionNotes: The radiating ray pattern easily distinguishes eastern lampmussels from most other freshwater mussels in New England, which typically have more uniform coloring or different shell shapes. Remember: rays = lampmussel, no rays = likely a different species entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'mussel,' freshwater mussels like the eastern lampmussel are completely unrelated to the marine mussels you might eat at a restaurant - they're actually more closely related to clams and belong to an entirely different family that evolved separately in freshwater environments.
compareHints: Eastern lampmussels have more pronounced and numerous radiating rays compared to their relatives like the Plain Pocketbook, which has a smoother, more uniform shell surface. The Yellow Lampmussel is typically more golden in color with less distinct rays. The eastern species also tends to be more elongated and less inflated than its lampmussel cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Plain Pocketbook lives up to its name by lacking the bright yellow color of the Yellow Lampmussel and the distinctive green rays of the Eastern Lampmussel.
Compared to its cousin the Eastern lampmussel, the yellow lampmussel has warmer, more golden tones and typically lacks the distinct greenish rays.
